## 08.6 Failure modes and graceful degradation

The architecture is designed around the assumption that **things will be down.** Each row is a failure the
tiers are meant to absorb (carried into the P16 robustness/security catalogue, chapter 13).

| Failure | What breaks | Graceful degradation |
|---------|-------------|----------------------|
| **Backhaul / cloud link down** (storm cuts gateway) | Tier 3 cellular, cloud ingest | Fall to Tier 2 LoRa mesh + Tier 1 siren; **DTN store-carry-forward** (Spray-and-Wait) queues and rebroadcasts until a link returns (`dtn.py`; F-10; **FM-11**, critical). |
| **Node dead** (fire destroys a sensor/relay) | mesh coverage shrinks, a path drops | Mesh re-routes via remaining nodes (position/energy-aware routing, 2510.03714); binary Spray-and-Wait still has copies on surviving nodes; **Tier 1 siren at each surviving site is independent.** |
| **Power brownout** | compute/radio intermittent | Battery/solar on Tier-1 siren keeps the local alarm alive; low-duty LoRa + duty-cycle discipline; nodes persist queued alerts (store) across restarts rather than losing them. |
| **RF jamming / DoS** | radio tiers suppressed | Multi-radio + spread-spectrum improves resilience (PDR>95% under jamming, **SIM**, 2603.02105); **Tier 1 siren is jam-proof** (physical); detect-and-report jamming via the P9/P10 network-anomaly layer. |
| **Density collapse** (dense fleeing crowd) | BLE mesh broadcast-storm collapse (1910.03345) | Cap hop count/TTL, rate-limit relays, position/energy-aware routing; do not rely on BLE as sole last-100 m. |
| **Spoofed cell broadcast** | fake "evacuate"/"all clear" (2604.24404) | Signed CAP + cross-cell corroboration + multi-channel agreement before acting; show unverified as UNVERIFIED only. |
| **Alert fatigue / cry-wolf** | compliance erodes (1904.01963) | Detection-precision gate before any wide tier; per-area false-alarm budget; persistence/dwell before escalation; **staggered** rollout (−70% to −89% social cost, 2606.30320); plain "Basic-Information" wording beats threat framing (2102.00589); logged suppression of chronically-flagging sources, surfaced to humans. |
| **No authority / certification** | cannot originate Tier 3 | Operate the owned Tiers 1/2/0; **request** an official alert from the authorized agency — never self-originate (Rule 19; autonomous public alert `[INFEASIBLE]`). |

Overriding rule: **fail-safe is to degrade to a lower, owned, physical tier and to "uncertain/offline"**,
never to go silent at the top and never to escalate autonomously (Rule 19).

---

# 09 — WS4: CCTV Fire/Smoke Detection + Edge Features

> **Scope of this chapter.** WS4 in the user documentation frame = internal workstream WS4 (phase P8, plus
> the zero-shot complement inserted as P14Z). Code packages: `trinetra/src/trinetra/ws4_cctv/` (numpy
> interface + temporal validator) and `trinetra/src/trinetra/deep/fire_cnn.py` (PyTorch spatiotemporal
> detector). This chapter follows `_CANON.md §3` (workstream mapping), `§5` (constraint C7, Rule 16/19/20),
> and `§6` (load-bearing verdicts). Every WS4 number that could look like a measured result of ours is
> **"not measured"**: no model in this program has been trained and no dataset has been downloaded
> (`_CANON.md §0`). Paper numbers are **SOURCE-REPORTED** and carry an arXiv ID.

---

## 9.1 The problem — early fire/smoke detection on *existing* CCTV, with few false alarms

The job of WS4 is narrow and concrete: turn cameras a site **already owns** (building CCTV, roadside
cameras, a cheap River-Eye node) into an early, *advisory* fire/smoke/disaster signal that a human operator
can trust, without flooding that operator with false alarms. Three things make this hard, and WS4 is
designed around them rather than around a headline accuracy number.

1. **False-alarm fatigue is the real adversary, not raw recall.** The evaluation protocol
   (`ws4_cctv/evaluation_protocol.md §1`) pre-registers an operating point of **≤ ~1 false alarm per
   camera-day** because the literature scan found that false-alarm fatigue — not missed-detection rate —
   dominates whether operators keep a detector switched on. A detector that fires on every sunset, every
   headlight, and every steam puff is worse than useless: it trains the operator to ignore it. Every design
   choice below (temporal persistence, cross-camera corroboration, physics gating, abstention) exists to
   buy down false alarms at a fixed sensitivity.

2. **The valuable case is the hardest case.** Early, small, translucent smoke — the onset you most want to
   catch — has the lowest contrast and is the easiest to miss
   (`ws4_cctv/failure_taxonomy.md §D`). A system tuned on big, obvious, late-stage flame will look
   excellent on a benchmark and fail at the one moment that matters. WS4 therefore reports time-to-detection
   and recall **separately for early/small vs established** fire, and refuses to average them away.

3. **The hardware is cheap and the sites are unseen.** The target edge is a two-tier split
   (`ws4_cctv/model_selection.md`): a tiny always-on gate on an ESP32-CAM/OV2640 class node (INT8,
   peak-SRAM-bound, high-recall) and a stronger small-YOLO-class detector on a Raspberry-Pi/phone-class
   gateway. A model that overfits one camera's lighting and background is near-worthless when deployed to a
   new site. Hence the central protocol rule (`§9.6`): judge on **held-out cameras and held-out sites**, not
   random frame splits.

### Privacy constraint C7 — raw video stays local

`_CANON.md §5` makes C7 a hard constraint: **no raw-video egress.** Operationally this means raw frames are
**scored at the edge** (on the node or the local gateway) and only *derived* signals — a calibrated
confidence, a time-to-detection estimate, a health/tamper flag — leave the camera. The research notes
(`ws4_cctv/plan.md §9`, `failure_taxonomy.md §F`) add on-device face/person blurring and data minimisation
by default, with an explicit test requirement that **blurring must not erase the smoke/flame evidence
itself**. This is why the `ws4_cctv` interface is built so the *false-alarm-suppressing logic*
(`TemporalValidator`) is pure numpy and runs wherever the frames already are, independent of the heavy
detector. C7 is a privacy requirement *and* an architecture driver, not a bolt-on.

> **Rule 19 (`_CANON.md §5`).** WS4 is advisory and human-in-the-loop. It emits a calibrated confidence into
> the fusion/alert layer; it **never** autonomously raises a public alarm. "Uncertain / offline / abstain"
> is a valid and preferred output under degradation.

---

## 9.2 Literature landscape (real arXiv IDs, all SOURCE-REPORTED)

The P8 reading logged **41 arXiv sources** plus **16** for the zero-shot complement P14Z
(`ws4_cctv/literature_map.md`). An important honesty caveat travels with all of them: **every one was read
at ABS (abstract/title/venue) depth — 0 full texts this phase**, the arXiv API was rate-limited, and paper
identities are subagent-reported and were not each independently re-fetched. Treat the IDs and numbers below
as **source-reported, ABS-level evidence**, never as established fact and never as ours.

**Fixed-camera early smoke + canonical baselines.** SmokeyNet on FIgLib/HPWREN (**2112.08598**, a CNN+LSTM+ViT
pipeline on ~25k fixed-view smoke images) is the canonical fixed-camera early-smoke reference and supplies
both a leakage-safe (per-camera/event) split idea and a time-to-detection reference. PYRONEAR-2025
(**2402.05349**) is a real-world, multi-site camera-network early-wildfire benchmark that motivates
site/camera-grouped splits and false-alarm estimation. An image-based early-detection system
(**2211.01629**, NeurIPS'22 CCCW) sits in the same ecosystem.

**Compact / edge detectors.** OnFire compact CNNs (**2010.08833**, ShuffleNetV2-/NasNet-A-OnFire;
src-reported 95% full-frame accuracy, 49 fps on Jetson Xavier-NX) is the best-documented true low-power
baseline, though it is non-temporal and therefore optimistic against CCTV nuisances. EFA-YOLO
(**2409.12635**; src-reported **1.4M params, 22.19 ms CPU**) is our edge-detector candidate (feature F-11). A
post-detection uncertainty/confidence-refinement head on YOLOv5n/v8n over D-Fire (**2510.10108**) names NMS
as a false-alarm failure mode.

**Temporal / motion validation.** The direct basis for our temporal validator is **2607.03131**
(multi-task surveillance + temporal event validation; src-reported false-alarm **52% → 4%**, <100 ms/frame)
— require an event to persist across frames before alarming. Dynamic-texture (3-orthogonal-plane CNN,
**1703.05530**), optical-flow + Swin + uncertainty smoke segmentation (**2508.14597**), and obscured-flame
via smoke motion (**2307.00104**) round out the temporal evidence. Note **2307.00104** reports "~100% video"
classification — flagged in `FEATURES.md` as F-24 **OVERFIT RED FLAG**, carried as a caution, not evidence.

**IR / thermal (RGB fails under smoke, at night).** Unsupervised IR fire/smoke segmentation
(**1909.12937**; src-reported 95.39% frame-level, no labels) underpins feature F-16. IR+thermal fusion
penetrating heavy smoke where RGB fails (**2307.04223**; src-reported mAP@0.5 95% on Jetson Nano) underpins
the parked thermal branch F-25. Supporting thermal references: WIT-UAS (**2312.09159**), FlameVQA RGB+
radiometric thermal (**2606.27128**), FLAME aerial RGB+IR (**2012.14036**).

**Compression / low-res robustness.** Learned compression measurably changes downstream fire segmentation
(**2512.01788**); SmokeBench surveillance desmoking targets the 0–15 min early-smoke regime (**2509.12701**);
Fire360 (**2506.02167**) is a degraded-visibility robustness-collapse regime. A two-stage adaptive
compression + detection cascade (**2508.16739**, IEEE JSTARS) underpins the parked UAV feature F-26.

**Protocol / leakage evidence.** A withdrawn CCTV smoking-detection paper (**2508.11696**) is a textbook
cautionary case: the authors withdrew it over augmentation-induced leakage across splits. A multi-scene FSD
benchmark (**2410.16631**) documents that public fire/smoke datasets lack standardised construction — the
field's bottleneck. Domain-adaptation / generalisation work (**2603.02465**) and a synthetic→real gap study
(**2511.16617**) reinforce the leakage-safe discipline. The overarching CV discipline — spatial-block (not
random) CV — is `_CANON.md §6`'s load-bearing verdict (arXiv 2608.22293).

**Trained vs zero-shot in the fire domain (the decisive evidence).** In fire specifically, trained detectors
**beat** zero-shot: WildFireCan-MMD's custom model scores 84.48% f-score **>** zero-shot VLMs
(**2504.13231**); AI4Fire found **no** core zero-shot model beat trivial baselines across 5 wildfire tasks
and documented leakage/label flaws (**2610.10946**); wildfire-PM2.5 foundation models lose to a trained
BiLSTM and show heavy-tailed OOD instability, including negative R² (**2607.07951**). Zero-shot CLIP is also
empirically miscalibrated (**2303.12748**), becomes over-confident under perturbation (**2512.12997**), and
confuses the exact fine-grained classes a fire system must separate — smoke vs steam/fog/dust
(**2404.03539**). This evidence is why zero-shot is admitted **only** as a calibrated low-weight complement
(`§9.5`, D-011).

A compact illustration of the overfit trap: SegNet drone wildfire detection (**2405.00031**) reports a
compact 5-conv/2-dense model at **98.18%** accuracy *but* an 11-conv/3-dense model at only 39.31% — more
capacity did *worse*. Per `FEATURES.md`, any **>98% single-split headline is treated as an overfit
candidate, not evidence.** We cite 2405.00031 for its design lesson (compact wins; resolution is a
safety-relevant hyperparameter), not for its headline number.

---

## 9.3 The implemented model — `deep/fire_cnn.py`, layer by layer, as in code

The reference implementation is `trinetra/src/trinetra/deep/fire_cnn.py` (Model 2). It is
**[CONFIRMED] `py_compile`-clean only; it has NOT been trained on a GPU in this environment** (`_CANON.md
§2`). Everything below is the architecture *as written in code*, not a trained result.

### Config (`FireNetConfig`)
```
in_ch = 3            # RGB
base = 32            # base channel width
gru_hidden = 128     # temporal state width
n_classes = 2        # [fire, smoke] — MULTI-LABEL (sigmoid, not softmax)
strouhal_weight = 0.0   # Class-C novel flicker term -> OFF by default (Rule 20)
```
`n_classes = 2` as **multi-label** matters: fire and smoke can co-occur or occur alone, so the head uses
independent sigmoids, not a softmax over mutually exclusive classes.

### Per-frame encoder (`FrameEncoder`)
A small 2-D CNN applied to every frame independently. Each `ConvBNAct` is `Conv2d(k=3,s=1,p=1, bias=False) →
BatchNorm2d → SiLU` (`deep/layers.py`). The stack:
```
ConvBNAct(3  -> 32)   -> MaxPool2d(2)      # H/2
ConvBNAct(32 -> 64)   -> MaxPool2d(2)      # H/4
ConvBNAct(64 -> 128)  -> MaxPool2d(2)      # H/8
ConvBNAct(128-> 128)  -> AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)   # global pool -> (B, 128, 1, 1)
```
Output `out_dim = base*4 = 128`; `forward` returns `(B, 128)` after `flatten(1)`. Three downsampling pools
then a global average pool keep it cheap and resolution-tolerant — appropriate for a gateway-class device.

### Temporal pathway + heads (`FireSmokeNet`)
Input is a **clip**, `x: (B, T, C, H, W)`. The forward pass, exactly as coded:
```
B,T,C,H,W = x.shape
feats = encoder(x.reshape(B*T, C, H, W)).reshape(B, T, 128)   # per-frame features
seq, hN = gru(feats)        # nn.GRU(128 -> gru_hidden=128), batch_first
h = hN.squeeze(0)           # last hidden state (B, 128)
logits  = head(h)           # nn.Linear(128 -> 2)  : [fire, smoke] logits
flick   = relu(flicker(h))  # nn.Linear(128 -> 1)  : flicker-frequency estimate (Hz), >= 0
return {"logits": logits, "prob": sigmoid(logits), "flicker_hz": flick}
```
So the model is **CNN encoder → GRU → {fire, smoke} multi-label logits**, plus an **auxiliary flicker-Hz
head**. The GRU is the design's core false-alarm suppressor: sun glint and headlights are single-frame
events; real fire **flickers persistently**, so a model that reads a short temporal window can separate them
in a way a single-frame classifier cannot. (The module docstring states this explicitly.)

### The Strouhal auxiliary head (Class-C, OFF by default)
`loss()` combines a standard multi-label BCE with an *optional* physics-consistency penalty:
```
bce = binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, targets, pos_weight)
total = bce
if cfg.strouhal_weight > 0 and plume_size_m is not None:     # gated, Class-C
    strou = strouhal_consistency_loss(flicker_hz, plume_size_m)   # f ~ 1.5/sqrt(D)
    total = total + cfg.strouhal_weight * strou
return {"loss": total, "bce": ..., "strouhal": ...}
```
`strouhal_consistency_loss` (`deep/losses.py`) penalises deviation of the predicted flicker frequency from
the Strouhal law **f ≈ 1.5 / √D** (D = plume diameter). This is a Class-A fire relation
(`_CANON.md §4`), but using it as a *novel* flicker regulariser is treated as **Class C** and is **gated OFF
by default** (`strouhal_weight = 0.0`), honouring Rule 20 (novel terms default-OFF with an A/B fallback).
Critically, the loss term is *consistency only* — the established-physics gate (Heskestad/Byram, in
`ws1a_firephys`) still runs separately at inference; this head never *replaces* the hard gate, it only
nudges training when explicitly enabled.

### How `ws4_cctv` maps a detector confidence to an `ExpertOutput`

`ws4_cctv/__init__.py` is deliberately split from the heavy model:

- `EdgeDetector` is an **interface stub**. Its `.detect(frame)` raises `MissingDependency` because the real
  frame-level backbone (YOLO-n class) needs torch, which is not installed in this sandbox (`_CANON.md §2`).
  The validator below works on **any** detector's confidence stream, which keeps the false-alarm logic
  usable at the edge without torch.
- `TemporalValidator` is **pure numpy** and is the false-alarm suppressor realised in code:
  ```
  TemporalValidator(window=5, min_frames=3, conf_thr=0.5)
  update(frame_conf):
      buf.append(frame_conf)                               # sliding window of last `window` confidences
      support = count(c >= conf_thr in buf)
      confirmed = support >= min_frames                    # must PERSIST
      conf = mean(c for c in buf if c >= conf_thr) if support else 0.0
      return ValidatedEvent(confirmed, confidence=conf if confirmed else 0.0, support_frames=support)
  ```
  It confirms an event only when per-frame confidence stays above `conf_thr` for at least `min_frames` of the
  last `window` frames — rejecting single-frame glints, headlights, and steam puffs. This is feature F-12 in
  its minimal, numpy form (`§9.4`).

The confidence then becomes a fusion expert via `ws5_fusion_rl/adapters.deep_expert(...)`. The adapter wraps
a scalar probability into the shared `ExpertOutput` dataclass (`common/types.py`: fields `p, source, u, c, r,
cls, available`, each in [0,1]) with a **source-appropriate trust cap**. The relevant policy rows
(`adapters._POLICY`):
```
"fire_cnn": (default r = 0.80, hard cap r = 0.95, cls = DATA)
"cctv":     (default r = 0.75, hard cap r = 0.90, cls = DATA)
```
So a CCTV/fire-CNN detector enters fusion as a **Class-DATA expert with a reliability ceiling** (never
treated as hard physics, cap < 1.0), carrying its calibrated probability `p`, an uncertainty `u`, a
physics-consistency `c`, and its reliability `r`. From there it flows through the single `decide()` path in
`ws5_fusion_rl` — advisory only, Rule 19. The adapter is torch-free on purpose so the offline gateway can
assemble experts from cached scores without importing torch.

### ASCII flow: frame → detector → temporal validation → fusion
```
  CCTV / River-Eye frames (RAW VIDEO STAYS LOCAL — C7)
          |
          v
 +--------------------------+     on-device, face/person blur, data-minimised
 | per-frame CNN encoder    |     (deep/fire_cnn.py: ConvBNAct x4 + pools)
 |  (B,T,3,H,W)->(B,T,128)  |
 +--------------------------+
          |  per-frame features
          v
 +--------------------------+     temporal pathway = key false-alarm suppressor
 | GRU(128->128) -> heads   |     fire flickers PERSISTENTLY; glint/headlight = 1 frame
 |  logits{fire,smoke}      |---> flicker_hz --(Strouhal aux, Class-C, OFF)--> consistency
 +--------------------------+
          |  sigmoid prob (per-frame conf stream)
          v
 +--------------------------+     ws4_cctv.TemporalValidator (pure numpy, F-12)
 | sliding window persist   |     window=5, min_frames=3, conf_thr=0.5
 | + cross-camera corrob.   |     + pre-registered cross-camera rule (F-11/F-12/F-16)
 +--------------------------+
          |  ValidatedEvent(confirmed, confidence)
          v
 +--------------------------+     ws5_fusion_rl.adapters.deep_expert("fire_cnn"/"cctv")
 | ExpertOutput (Class DATA |     reliability CAPPED (0.90-0.95); u,c,r attached
 |  p,u,c,r; r<=cap)        |
 +--------------------------+
          |     joins physics (Heskestad/Byram gate), IoT, anomaly, zero-shot(low wt)
          v
 +--------------------------+     ws5_fusion_rl.decide()  --  ADVISORY ONLY (Rule 19)
 | meta-fusion -> Decision  |     level = max(conformal_level(risk,p*), shield_floor)
 | human operator decides   |     NEVER an autonomous public alert
 +--------------------------+
```

## 9.4 Edge features — F-11, F-12, F-16 (approved-for-build-plan) + parked F-25, F-26

All five are from `FEATURES.md`. All evidence is ABS-level and SOURCE-REPORTED; **none is built or tested**,
and each approved feature carries a **pre-registered cross-camera/cross-site decision rule** — a feature that
helps one benchmark but hurts cross-camera performance is **not** a win (gated via the inferential-
reproducibility test 2302.04054).

### F-11 — EFA-YOLO efficient edge detector `[approved-for-build-plan]`
- **What it does.** An attention-lite + depthwise-separable small YOLO backbone for the gateway detector —
  the main fire+smoke detector on Pi/phone-class hardware.
- **Evidence.** 2409.12635, src-reported **1.4M params, 22.19 ms CPU**.
- **Planned cost.** Low (single-GPU retrain; CPU-real-time inference).
- **Pre-registered decision rule.** Keep **only if cross-CAMERA mAP gain > seed variance** vs the current
  backbone. **Risk (explicit):** micro-architecture mAP gains often shrink cross-camera — a single-split
  overfit trap.

### F-12 — Temporal multi-frame event validation `[approved-for-build-plan]`
- **What it does.** Confidence-weighted voting + cascade filter requiring an event to **persist** before
  alarming. This is exactly what `ws4_cctv.TemporalValidator` implements in minimal numpy form, and what the
  GRU pathway in `fire_cnn.py` learns in its trained form.
- **Evidence.** 2607.03131, src-reported **false alarms 52% → 4%**, <100 ms/frame.
- **Planned cost.** Very low (post-processor, no retrain).
- **Pre-registered decision rule.** Keep if the false-alarm reduction **holds cross-site at matched
  sensitivity**. **Risk:** framerate/latency-to-alert tradeoff; it **must not raise the missed-event rate**.

### F-16 — Unsupervised IR optical-flow / flicker physics feature `[approved-for-build-plan]`
- **What it does.** A label-free classical-CV feature (optical-flow / flicker-band physics) for cold-start,
  before any labels exist — ties the Strouhal/flicker physics into a cheap on-node cue.
- **Evidence.** 1909.12937, src-reported **95.39% frame-level, no labels**.
- **Planned cost.** Very low (classical CV, no GPU/labels).
- **Pre-registered decision rule.** Keep if it **adds signal over RGB-only on cross-site video**. **Risk:**
  sensitive to framerate/codec/PTZ motion.

### Pre-registered cross-camera decision rule (shared)
Per `FEATURES.md §P17` and `ws4_cctv/evaluation_protocol.md §2`, every WS4 feature is admitted only if its
improvement **exceeds seed/trial variance on a HELD-OUT CROSS-CAMERA / CROSS-SITE split** *and* its cost is
justified. Splits are grouped by **site → camera → video** (all frames of a video in one split; whole
cameras/sites held out), with the cross-site tier as the headline. This rule is fixed **before** any build so
results cannot be shopped.

### Parked features (reasons stated)
- **F-25 — Thermal/IR fusion branch for low-visibility** `[proposed / parked]`. Evidence 2307.04223
  (src-reported mAP@0.5 95% on Jetson Nano). Low inference cost **but requires IR hardware + a calibration
  rig**. Parked because it is **gated on IR hardware availability + the ≤₹2000 node cap (C2)** and **likely
  exceeds the prototype budget**. IR fusion is the designed remedy for the night/fog/smoke-occlusion failure
  modes (`§9.7`) — but only when the hardware budget allows it. `[HYPOTHESIS]` for our deployment until BOM
  verified in P6.
- **F-26 — Two-stage UAV adaptive compression + policy early-exit** `[proposed / parked]`. Evidence
  2508.16739 (src-reported large compute cut). **High cost** — needs an RL-style policy net + orchestration.
  Parked: **defer until the core detector is validated.**

---

## 9.5 Design choices + rejected/deferred alternatives

**Chosen: two-stage cascade (tiny on-node gate → gateway detector) + temporal confirmation + physics/
cross-modal fusion.** (`ws4_cctv/model_selection.md`.) Rationale: the edge is genuinely two-tier
(ESP32-CAM is INT8-tiny-model-only; a Pi/phone-class gateway can host a real detector), and false-alarm
control is decisive. The on-node gate is tuned for **high recall** (don't miss, tolerate false positives it
passes up); the gateway detector and temporal stage buy the precision back.

**Trained detector = PRIMARY; zero-shot = LOW-WEIGHT CALIBRATED COMPLEMENT (decision D-011).**
(`ws4_cctv/zero_shot_design.md`, `_CANON.md §6`, `FINAL_REPORT.md` line 26.) The evidence that trained beats
zero-shot *in the fire domain* is specific and strong: 2504.13231 (custom 84.48% f-score > zero-shot VLMs),
2610.10946 (no core zero-shot model beat trivial baselines, documented leakage), 2607.07951 (foundation
models lose to a trained BiLSTM, negative-R² OOD tail). Zero-shot is admitted **only** for open-vocab /
unknown-hazard breadth the closed-set detector was never trained on, and only after **mandatory calibration
before fusion** (one temperature per backbone, 2303.12748; Dirichlet uncertainty, 2512.12997; feed entropy/
prob-difference, not raw softmax; de-rate external numbers for leakage up to 8.9%, 2107.13029). It enters
fusion at **low weight**, never as the primary detector.

**Rejected / deferred alternatives (with evidence):**
- **Classical cues alone (color/motion/flicker).** Cheap and interpretable but weak alone → **kept only as a
  cheap on-node gate + physics-consistency check, not standalone.**
- **DETR / transformer detector.** Strong global context but heavy → **server tier only, not an edge node.**
- **Open-vocabulary / foundation detector as the primary.** Zero-shot prompts but large and, per the fire
  evidence above, weaker than trained → **deferred to the P14Z low-weight complement.**
- **Zero-shot as the detector.** Rejected by D-011 on the fire-domain evidence + miscalibration.
- **Anomaly/one-class on video as the detector.** Not a detector; **handed to WS8** as the explicit target
  for the supervised detector's blind spots.
- **Over-deep CNNs.** 2405.00031 shows an 11-conv/3-dense model *underperforming* a compact 5-conv/2-dense
  one — capacity is not free; `fire_cnn.py` is deliberately compact.

---

## 9.6 Evaluation — pre-registered protocol; our results = "not measured"

The protocol (`ws4_cctv/evaluation_protocol.md`) was pre-registered **before** any model was built, so
results cannot be shopped. **No WS4 detection number is measured by us** (Rule 16) — the items below are the
*bar*, not claimed as met.

- **Leakage-safe splits (the central rule).** Group by **site → camera → video**; all frames of a video stay
  in one split; whole cameras/sites held out. Three tiers: within-site, **cross-camera**, **cross-site**
  (cross-site is the headline). Temporal ordering where timestamps exist (test videos later than train).
  **Never** random-frame splits — the withdrawn paper 2508.11696 is the cautionary case.
- **False alarms per camera-day** at the fixed operating point (**≤ ~1/camera-day** target), measured on the
  nuisance negatives from the failure taxonomy — reported, not just recall.
- **Time-to-detection** (median + full distribution), **split by difficulty**: early/small smoke reported
  separately and honestly even when worse than established fire.
- **Calibration:** reliability diagram + ECE, so the fusion/alert layer can trust the confidence it receives
  (this is why the `ExpertOutput` reliability cap exists).
- **Robustness curves:** metric vs JPEG/H.264 bitrate, vs resolution, vs night/IR.
- **Confidence intervals over ≥5 seeds** for every headline number — report CIs, not point values.
- **Baselines & variants on identical splits/seeds:** classical cues → single-frame deep → deep+temporal →
  physics-informed → cross-modal (camera + IoT). Reproduce published YOLO-family fire/smoke baselines first.

**On citing SOTA.** Published fire/smoke numbers mostly use random (often leakage-prone) splits, so they are
**not directly comparable** to our leakage-safe numbers. When we cite SOTA we say "source-reported under
their protocol" and re-run baselines under *this* protocol for an apples-to-apples reference.

**Overfit red-flags called out.** Per `FEATURES.md`, any **>98% single-split headline is an overfit
candidate, not evidence.** Named cases: 2307.00104's "~100% video" (feature F-24) and 2405.00031's 98.18%
single-dataset accuracy. We do not carry these as performance evidence.

**Our results, stated plainly:** `[CONFIRMED]` the numpy core (incl. `ws4_cctv.TemporalValidator`) runs
inside the 128-test / 6-gate suite and `fire_cnn.py` is `py_compile`-clean; **[not measured]** any detection
mAP, recall, false-alarm rate, time-to-detection, or calibration number for TRINETRA — no training, no
dataset.

---

## 9.7 Failure modes + mitigations

From `ws4_cctv/failure_taxonomy.md` (a test-design artifact; mitigations are **design requirements**, not
performance claims). The taxonomy also notes an honest gap: dedicated camera-tamper/blinding/replay-spoofing
and privacy papers for fire CCTV were **essentially absent** in the arXiv-only search (only 2412.20006 on
prediction-model adversarial robustness) → carried as an open action for non-arXiv follow-up, with the
WS2/P11 deepfake handoff covering replay-spoofing conceptually.

| Failure mode | Why it fools a detector | Mitigation (design requirement) |
|---|---|---|
| **Night / low light** | flame visible, smoke invisible | **IR/thermal branch (F-25, budget-gated)**; different nuisances (heaters/hot sun) handled separately |
| **Fog / cloud / haze** | gray diffuse regions mimic smoke (hardest smoke nuisance) | temporal **growth** check + sky-region priors; cross-modal IoT PM sensor; abstain under low confidence |
| **Steam / water vapor** | looks like white smoke | multi-class benign-vs-dangerous smoke; extinction/color priors; temporal growth |
| **Occlusion (foliage/structures)** | partial smoke/flame | multi-view / cross-camera **persistence** (the TemporalValidator's cross-camera corroboration); obscured-flame via smoke motion (2307.00104, with its red-flag) |
| **Camera shake / PTZ** | global motion mimics plume motion | motion compensation; temporal confirmation |
| **Compression (H.264/H.265), low-res** | blocking/blur destroys smoke texture | evaluate at realistic bitrates (robustness curves, §9.6); 2512.01788 shows compression changes outcomes |
| **Camera tamper / blinding (laser/IR)** | sensor saturation, blind spot | detect saturation + scene-change; **health/tamper flag; abstain** (fail-safe, Rule 19) |
| **Replayed-video spoofing** | fake "all clear" or fake alarm | stream liveness/integrity + signed streams → **WS2 deepfake handoff (P11)** |
| **Adversarial patch** | suppress/trigger detection | robustness tests + **cross-modal voting** so vision alone can't be gamed (2412.20006) |

**IR fusion gating on hardware/budget.** IR/thermal (F-25) is the designed answer to the night/fog/smoke-
occlusion cluster — thermal penetrates heavy smoke where RGB fails (2307.04223). But it is **gated on IR
hardware availability + the ≤₹2000 node cap (C2)** and is expected to exceed the prototype budget. So in the
baseline RGB-only build, the mitigation for those modes is **abstention + cross-modal corroboration (IoT
gas/heat) + temporal/cross-camera persistence**, with IR added only where the budget and hardware allow.
Privacy (C7): on-device processing + face/person blur + data minimisation, with a test that blurring does
not erase smoke/flame evidence.

# 10 — WS5: Offline-RL Advisory Alarm Policy, OPE Admission Gate, and Safety Shield

> Workstream scheme (per `_CANON.md §3`): this is the **user-frame WS5 = RL**, backed by code packages
> `trinetra/src/trinetra/ws5_fusion_rl/rl.py` (numpy core) and `trinetra/src/trinetra/deep/offline_rl.py`
> (PyTorch Model 6), with the Kaggle trainer `trinetra/kaggle/train_offline_rl.py`. The internal research
> artifacts live in `ws5_rl/` (phase P15). Do not confuse this WS5 with the *internal* "WS5 fusion" that
> `_CANON.md` also lists under the WS1 doc-frame — the package name `ws5_fusion_rl` carries both the fusion
> head and the RL policy, which is why the folder is dual-named.

> **Reality check first (read before any number below).** No TRINETRA RL policy has been trained, and no RL
> logs have been collected or downloaded. Per `_CANON.md §0`/`§2`: the numpy baseline + OPE gate in `rl.py`
> runs and is covered by the 128-test suite `[CONFIRMED]`; `deep/offline_rl.py` and the Kaggle trainer are
> **`py_compile`-clean only — never executed on a GPU here** `[CONFIRMED` that it compiles; the *training*
> is `not measured]`. Every quantitative claim about an algorithm in this chapter is **source-reported** from
> a cited paper on *that paper's own* (mostly D4RL / robotics / driving) benchmark — never a TRINETRA result.
> Where you expect a TRINETRA number, the honest answer is **"not measured."**

---

## 10.1 The problem — sequential alarm/escalation/maintenance under cost asymmetry

TRINETRA's decision layer must repeatedly answer a small but high-stakes question: given the current fused
hazard picture, **what alarm level do we advise the human dispatcher to consider** — and when do we escalate,
hold, or schedule maintenance? This is a *sequential decision problem under a sharply asymmetric cost model*.
A missed hazard in a life-safety mountain-disaster setting is catastrophic; a false alarm is costly
(cry-wolf fatigue, wasted dispatch) but recoverable. The canonical cost ratio carried by this project is
`C_FA = 5`, `C_miss = 100` (a missed event is ~20× worse than a false alarm), which fixes the optimal
alarm operating point at the probability threshold

```
p* = C_FA / (C_FA + C_miss) = 5 / 105 ≈ 0.0476
```

(`_CANON.md §4`). That same `0.0476` is the default threshold of the implemented `RuleBaselinePolicy`
(`rl.py:22`), so the rule baseline and the cost model are deliberately the *same* operating point expressed
two ways. The teaching point: the decision is not "classify risk accurately" but "**act under a loss where
the two error types are priced 20:1**," and a policy that is merely more accurate can still be worse if it
trades a cheap false alarm for an expensive miss (`FEATURES.md`/`FINAL_REPORT.md`: *"better prediction ≠
better decision,"* decision-focused-learning review 2606.21773).

**Why reinforcement learning at all, and why *offline*?** Three forces push toward RL and simultaneously
forbid the usual way of doing it:

1. **The decision is sequential and stateful.** Alarm/escalation/maintenance choices interact over time
   (escalating now changes what "hold" means later; deferred maintenance degrades future sensing). A policy
   that reasons about downstream consequences, not just the instantaneous label, is the natural object.
2. **We cannot explore in a live life-safety system.** Online RL *learns by trying actions and observing
   outcomes* — ethically and legally impossible when the "environment" is a populated valley. You cannot
   issue a real alarm to see what reward you get. This is the defining constraint of the whole workstream.
3. **We only have logged / simulated data.** The honest regime is therefore **offline (batch) RL**: learn a
   policy *purely* from a fixed dataset of `(state, action, reward, next_state)` tuples produced by some
   logging/behavior policy, with **no new interaction**. The canonical hazard of this regime is
   *distributional shift* — the learned policy wants to visit `(state, action)` pairs the logging policy
   rarely took, where bootstrapped value estimates are unreliable (offline-RL survey, Levine et al.
   2005.01643). Everything downstream (conservatism, the OPE gate, the shield) exists to tame that hazard.

The governing posture, carried verbatim from the canon and the research program, is **Rule 19: the RL output
is ADVISORY — ranked options surfaced to a human dispatcher, NEVER actuation** (`_CANON.md §5`;
`ws5_rl/rl_design.md §0`,`§7`; `FINAL_REPORT.md §1 WS5`). The policy may *recommend*; a human alone decides on
public dissemination.

---

## 10.2 The environment / MDP design — and the explicit BUILD GAP

### 10.2.1 The MDP as specified (design only — nothing simulated)

`ws5_rl/environment_spec.md` and `rl_design.md` specify, on paper, the Markov decision process the later build
would construct. **Nothing here is built or simulated** (research Rule 16); it is a specification.

- **State** (`environment_spec.md §2`): the fused risk estimate **and its uncertainty**, plus — for the full
  evacuation framing — population/crowd distribution, road-network graph, resource positions, sensor/camera
  coverage, and time. Partial observability (imperfect sensor coverage) is treated as the *realistic* case,
  not an edge case. In the *implemented* code the state is an abstract `state_dim`-vector (default 16;
  `CQLConfig.state_dim=16` in `offline_rl.py:26`) whose columns are the fused-risk / uncertainty / resource /
  time features — the code does not hard-code their semantics, it consumes whatever the logged dataset
  provides (`RLTransitionDataset`, `datamodules.py:99`).
- **Actions.** Two action framings coexist, and the gap between them is worth understanding:
  - The *implemented Model-6* action set is **discrete `{HOLD, WATCH, ALARM}`** — three alarm/escalation
    levels (`offline_rl.py:21`, `ACTIONS`). Ordering them `HOLD < WATCH < ALARM` is what makes the shield
    (10.5) a *monotone* "raise toward safety" operation.
  - The *numpy baseline* `RuleBaselinePolicy.act` is **binary** (`0 = hold`, `1 = alarm`; `rl.py:25-26`).
    `[LIKELY]` the 3-level CQL policy and the binary rule baseline are reconciled by mapping
    `{HOLD}→0, {WATCH,ALARM}→1` at the OPE comparison, but the code does not state the mapping explicitly —
    flagged as an open consistency point (see 10.9).
  - The *full research framing* additionally contemplates routing/allocation/dispatch and
    sensor/camera-control actions (`rl_design.md §0`), but those are the evacuation-env ambition, not the
    implemented alarm policy.
- **Reward.** Derived from the **cost-loss model** — penalize misses far more than false alarms, with hard
  safety-constraint terms and a *low-variance* preference (`environment_spec.md §2`; `rl_design.md §3`,
  variance-averse posture 2610.07899). The reward must price false alarms above a flat penalty to avoid
  cry-wolf (literature brief DC-18). In the implemented trainer the reward is simply the logged `r` column
  (`RLTransitionDataset.r`); the cost-loss shaping is a *data-generation* responsibility, not something the
  Q-net invents.
- **Termination:** evacuation complete / timeout / infeasible — where "infeasible" triggers a
  **minimum-predicted-peak-harm fallback** (FAITH 2610.12432) rather than undefined behavior.

### 10.2.2 The BUILD GAP (explicit, load-bearing)

**There is no off-the-shelf disaster-evacuation RL environment.** This is stated three times across the
artifacts and must not be softened: `environment_spec.md §1` ("no off-the-shelf disaster-evacuation env
surfaced in the throttled search"), `rl_design.md §2` ("HONEST GAP"), and `FINAL_REPORT.md §1 WS5` /
`§13` ("Build the disaster-evacuation RL environment (no off-the-shelf env exists — BUILD GAP)"). The
research position is **REUSE-over-BUILD**: wrap existing components rather than author a simulator from
scratch — crowd dynamics (Ctrl-CWM 2610.09438, or the open cinemere/evacuation Vicsek env 2509.19972),
fire-spread (PyroStack data 2609.36315 + FireGen stochastic sim 2610.07431), human evacuate/stay behavior
(FLARE 2502.17701), and JAX vectorization patterns (Crazyflow 2610.08225, BluffJAX 2610.07686) — with the
**only genuine build task** being a thin Gymnasium/PettingZoo wrapper unifying them. Every reuse candidate's
license and code availability is **`[LIKELY]` / to-be-VERIFIED at build**, not confirmed. Simulator outputs
are to be treated as *hypotheses* and validated against real fire progression (PyroStack) and real evacuation
behavior (FLARE) before any policy is trusted (`environment_spec.md §3`, sim-to-real caution 2610.05819).

## 10.3 The implemented policy — code, layer by layer

### 10.3.1 `deep/offline_rl.py` — Conservative Q-Learning (Model 6, PyTorch)

The implemented learner is **discrete-action Conservative Q-Learning (CQL)** (`offline_rl.py`, module
docstring; algorithm from Kumar et al. 2006.04779). It is `py_compile`-clean and **never GPU-trained here**
`[CONFIRMED]`. Walking the code as written:

- **`CQLConfig`** (`:24-31`): `state_dim=16`, `n_actions=3`, `hidden=(256,256)`, **`gamma=0.0`**,
  `cql_alpha=1.0`, `tau=0.005`. The default `gamma=0.0` is the design's single most important choice: it
  **collapses the MDP to a one-step contextual bandit** (docstring: *"Set gamma=0 for the one-step
  contextual-bandit variant (recommended when transitions are weakly Markov)"*). This is how the code
  reconciles "we implemented CQL" with the literature's "prefer one-step on small, narrow data" (10.5) —
  CQL *with γ=0* is a conservative one-step learner; `γ>0` turns on sequential bootstrapping only if the data
  justify it.
- **`QNet`** (`:34-40`): a single `MLP([state_dim, 256, 256, n_actions], norm=True)` — the Q-head maps a
  state vector to one Q-value per action. This is a **tiny network** (state × two 256-wide layers × 3
  actions); its size is the justification for single-GPU training (10.6).
- **`CQLPolicy`** (`:43-86`): holds an `online` QNet and a frozen `target` QNet (Polyak-averaged).
  - **`cql_loss`** (`:55-65`) is the training objective and the heart of the method:
    - `q_sa = Q(s)[a]` — the Q-value of the action actually taken in the data.
    - `target = r + γ·(1−done)·max_a' Q_target(s_next, a')` — the standard Bellman backup, computed under
      `no_grad` from the target net; with `γ=0` this is just the immediate reward `r`.
    - `bellman = MSE(q_sa, target)` — fit the taken-action value.
    - `conservative = mean(logsumexp_a Q(s,a) − q_sa)` — **the CQL penalty**. `logsumexp` is a soft-max over
      *all* actions; subtracting the data action's value and pushing the whole term down forces Q to be
      *low on out-of-distribution actions* and *relatively higher on observed actions*. This is exactly
      Kumar et al.'s mechanism for a **lower-bounded, conservative** Q that will not hallucinate value for a
      never-observed alarm action in a rare disaster state (`2006.04779` note, "Relevance to us").
    - `loss = bellman + cql_alpha · conservative`.
  - **`polyak_update`** (`:67-70`): `target ← (1−τ)·target + τ·online`, the slow target-net tracking that
    stabilizes bootstrapping.
  - **`act`** (`:72-81`): greedy `argmax_a Q(s)` **then raised to the shield floor** via
    `torch.maximum(greedy, shield_floor_idx)` — this is the post-posed safety shield in code (10.5).
  - **`action_probs`** (`:83-86`): `softmax(Q(s)/temperature)` — a *stochastic* target policy, needed so the
    OPE importance ratios in `rl.py` are well defined.

### 10.3.2 `ws5_fusion_rl/rl.py` — numpy baseline, policy interface, OPE, admission gate

This is the **runnable, test-covered numpy core** `[CONFIRMED]` (no torch dependency). It deliberately
implements *everything except the learned network itself*, so the honest fallback and the admission logic
work even in an environment with only numpy.

- **`RuleBaselinePolicy`** (`:19-26`): "alarm iff fused risk ≥ `threshold`," default `threshold=0.0476`
  (= `p*`). This is the **fixed-threshold policy a learned policy must BEAT**, and the fail-safe the system
  reverts to. Teaching point: the comparator is not a strawman — it is the Bayes-optimal threshold for the
  stated cost ratio, so beating it is a genuine bar.
- **`OfflineRLPolicy`** (`:29-39`): an *interface stub*. `fit()` raises `MissingDependency` with the message
  that the learned algo *"needs d3rlpy+torch (not installed). Until trained+OPE-admitted, the system uses
  RuleBaselinePolicy (Rule 19 fail-safe)."* This is intentional: in the numpy sandbox there is no trained
  policy, so the code *forces* the fail-safe rather than silently pretending.
- **`wis_value(behavior_probs, target_probs, rewards)`** (`:42-54`): **Weighted Importance Sampling** value
  estimate for one-step (contextual-bandit) OPE. It forms ratios `w = clip(t/clip(b,1e-6,None), 0, 1e3)`,
  returns `value = Σ(w·r)/Σw` and the **effective sample size** `ess = (Σw)² / Σ(w²)`. The ratio clipping
  and the ESS are the honest-statistics guardrails: WIS is only as trustworthy as its weights are
  well-behaved.
- **`ope_feasible(behavior_probs, …)`** (`:57-65`): the **positivity + ESS gate**. Returns `False` if any
  logged action probability is below `min_prob=1e-2` (a *positivity violation* — the logging policy almost
  never took some action, so no amount of reweighting can estimate its value) or if the ESS falls below
  `min_ess_frac=0.1` of the sample count (the estimate rests on too few effective samples). This is the
  gate that makes OPE *refuse to answer* when it cannot answer honestly (ties research FM-08,
  `literature_brief.md`).
- **`ope_admission(...)` → `OPEVerdict`** (`:68-83`): the deploy gate. It computes the target value
  `v_t` (via `wis_value`), the baseline value `v_b = mean(baseline_rewards)`, checks `feasible`, and sets

  ```
  deploy_learned = feasible AND v_t >= v_b
  ```

  i.e. **deploy the learned policy only if OPE is feasible AND its estimated value is at least the
  baseline's.** Otherwise the verdict keeps the rule baseline. This is Rule 19's fail-safe compiled into a
  boolean.

### 10.3.3 `kaggle/train_offline_rl.py` — how the two halves meet

The trainer (`train_offline_rl.py`, 81 lines, `py_compile`-clean, **not GPU-run** `[CONFIRMED]`) wires the
PyTorch learner to the numpy gate: it builds `CQLPolicy` from the data's `state_dim`, trains with AdamW +
gradient clipping + `polyak_update` per step (default `gamma=0.0`, `epochs=50`, `batch=256`), saves
`offline_rl.pt`, then — crucially — runs the **same `ope_admission` from `ws5_fusion_rl`** on the learned
policy's `action_probs` against the logged behavior probabilities and realized rewards. The report JSON
records `deploy_learned`; its own note strings make the gate explicit: *"DEPLOY learned policy
(OPE-admitted); still shielded upward at inference"* vs *"KEEP RuleBaselinePolicy — OPE did not admit the
learned policy (Rule 19 fail-safe)."* The baseline rewards passed in are the **logged behavior policy's own
realized rewards** (`train_offline_rl.py:66`) — a conservative choice (10.9).

### 10.3.4 The post-posed hard shield (floor can only raise)

The shield is **post-posed** (Alshiekh et al. 1708.08611, Fig. 2): the learned policy picks an action
*normally*, and the shield **corrects it only upward toward safety**. In code this is one line —
`torch.maximum(greedy, shield_floor_idx)` in `CQLPolicy.act` (`offline_rl.py:79-81`) — and it is *monotone*:
because actions are ordered `HOLD(0) < WATCH(1) < ALARM(2)`, the shield can only **raise** the alarm level to
a physics/sensor-derived floor, **never lower it**. This is the formal expression of *"it can only be
overridden UPWARD toward safety, never used to silence a hazard"* (`offline_rl.py` docstring; `_CANON.md §4`
`level = max(conformal_level(risk, p*), shield_floor)`). The shield floor is set by hard physics predicates
(e.g. FS<1, tilt>5°/day, 24h-rain>150mm, GLOF signature — see the shielding note and chapter 06), which are
*independent of the learned model*, satisfying Rule 19's requirement for hard guardrails that do not depend
on a learned component. **Realizability caveat `[LIKELY]`:** `FEATURES.md` F-06 requires the shield to be
*realizability-checked* (2507.23603) — i.e. the conjunction of physics predicates must not be contradictory
(FM-05, conflicting FS/tilt/rain/GLOF rules). The numpy `rl.py` does not implement the shield object itself;
the shield is the `shield_floor_idx` argument + the physics layer (chapter 06). Flagged as a composition
point in 10.9.

---

## 10.4 The honest OPE / valuation protocol (deploy gate)

The *implemented* gate (10.3.2) is deliberately a **minimal one-step WIS + positivity/ESS** check — exactly
what is defensible in a numpy-only, no-trained-policy environment. The *pre-registered research-grade
valuation protocol* is broader and is specified in `TRINETRA_Workstreams.md` (WS2 evaluation task 4,
"Honest RL valuation") and `ws5_rl/rl_evaluation_plan.md`. It uses **real arXiv method references**, carried
exactly as named (these four are cited in `TRINETRA_Workstreams.md:53-56`; they have **no local paper note**,
so no numbers are attributed to them here — method names only):

- **Policy selection by BVFT** (Batch Value-Function Tournament, **arXiv 2110.14000**): choose among candidate
  policies *offline*, by a value-function tournament, rather than by online return — because we cannot tune
  online.
- **Risk evaluation by SCOPE-RL** (**arXiv 2311.18206**): report **CVaR@5% (worst-case tail)**, worst-case
  return, and the *full return distribution*, not just the mean — the correct posture when the tail is a
  mass-casualty event.
- **A one-step offline baseline reported alongside** (**arXiv 2106.08909**, Brandfonbrener et al.) and
  **arXiv 2206.02000** as the companion valuation reference.
- **Deploy-gate:** *"deploy only if the OPE lower bound ≥ rule baseline"* (`TRINETRA_Workstreams.md:55`) —
  the research statement of the same `v_t ≥ v_b` gate the code implements, strengthened to a *lower bound*.
- **Feedback-aware OPE** (**arXiv 2312.01530**, `TRINETRA_Workstreams.md:56`): model
  evacuation/alarm/maintenance *feedback* in the OPE, because the action changes the future data.

Supporting method anchors from the paper notes: use **FQE/OPE to RANK policies offline, iterate only if OPE
is feasible** (Model-Selection-for-Offline-RL 2107.11003, `literature_brief.md`); OPE is a *named open
problem* in the field (offline-RL survey 2005.01643), so the whole RL approach is **gated on OPE quality**,
not assumed to work. This valuation plumbing — BVFT selection, SCOPE-RL CVaR, one-step comparator,
feedback-aware OPE, lower-bound deploy gate — is **spec/plan only; `not measured`.**

---

## 10.5 Algorithm alternatives considered (evidence + decision)

The research program treated the offline-RL algorithm as an explicit comparison, **CR-03** (multi-stage/
iterative vs simple one-step), with source-reported evidence. All numbers below are the cited paper's own
results on *their* benchmarks (D4RL locomotion unless noted) — **not TRINETRA measurements**:

| Candidate | What it is | Source-reported evidence (that paper's benchmark) | Role here |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| **CQL** (2006.04779) | Conservative Q, lower-bounds OOD-action value | abstract claims 2–5× higher return vs prior offline methods; strongest on multimodal data (exact D4RL rows not seen, `[ABS/FT-PARTIAL]`) | **Implemented** Model 6; conservatism is the safety mechanism |
| **TD3+BC** (2106.06860) | TD3 + a behavior-cloning term + state normalization | Hopper-Medium 99.5±1.0 vs CQL 72.0; Walker2d-Medium 79.7±1.8 vs CQL 30.1; HalfCheetah-Medium 42.8±0.3 vs CQL 37.4; "~2× faster" | Minimalist parsimony baseline; `FEATURES.md` F-06 names it "baseline-first" |
| **IQL** (2110.06169) | Expectile value, *never queries OOD actions* | claims SOTA on D4RL (exact rows pruned, `[FT-PARTIAL]`) | Attractive for safety (cannot be seduced by unobserved (state,alarm) pairs) |
| **One-step** (2106.08909) | One step of improvement on an on-policy Q^β, **no OPE** | one-step beats multi/iterative on most mujoco-medium (halfcheetah-m 55.6 vs 40.8 vs 47.4; walker2d-m 85.6 vs 75.9 vs 75.4; hopper-m 83.3 vs 53.0 vs 54.2); **iterative wins only on large, well-covered (random) data** | The decisive argument for small/narrow data |
| SAC (1801.01290) / PPO (1707.06347) | Online max-entropy / on-policy PG | SAC: stable across seeds; PPO: multiple epochs per batch (ABS-only, body unreadable) | **Online** — only a *simulator-stage-4* option; dangerous on a live alarm system → effectively ruled out |

**The decision, and why.** The literature's parsimony lesson is strong and consistent: on **small,
narrow-coverage** data (which disaster logs certainly are — few real events), **OPE is unreliable, so
iterative actor-critic methods that repeatedly do OPE amplify its variance** (2106.08909 diagnosis;
reinforced by TD3+BC's "simple rivals CQL" result and the survey's OPE open-problem). That is why:

- The **default is one-step** (`CQLConfig.gamma=0.0` makes the implemented CQL a *one-step* conservative
  learner — the code embodies "prefer simple" without discarding the conservatism machinery).
- CQL was chosen as the implemented *form* because its conservative penalty is a clean, single-coefficient
  way to keep a discrete-action policy inside the logging support — the property that matters most for a
  safety policy — and it degrades gracefully to one-step at `γ=0`.
- Escalation to full iterative CQL/IQL (`γ>0`) is **conditional on demonstrating large coverage** — which
  we probably cannot (2106.08909 guidance; `literature_brief.md` staged policy: *fixed threshold → one-step
  offline RL → iterative only if OPE-feasible*).
- Online methods (SAC/PPO) are **ruled out for deployment** because they require exploration in a live
  life-safety system; PPO is "the Stage-4 online fine-tuning option in a simulator, if at all" (PPO note).

Note a documented **design-vs-code divergence `[LIKELY]`**: `FEATURES.md` F-06 lists the component as
"Offline RL alarm policy (**TD3-BC** baseline-first)" citing 2106.08909/2506.00505, while the *implemented*
Model 6 is **CQL**. These are consistent in spirit (both are "simple, support-respecting offline RL"), and
the staged plan permits either; but a reader comparing F-06 to `offline_rl.py` should know the implemented
algorithm is CQL (one-step by default), not TD3+BC. See 10.9.

## 10.6 Compute budget — the ~30 GPU-h Kaggle frame and why RL is ~1.0 GPU-h on one GPU

Project-wide, Kaggle is assumed **~30 GPU-h/week**, kept to **~25.5 usable** after a ≥15% reserve
(`_CANON.md §8`; `KAGGLE_BUDGET.md`). Within that envelope, **WS5 RL/alarm is budgeted at ≈ 1.0 GPU-h**,
with the explicit lever *"OPE/FQE on logged/sim episodes … offline eval mostly CPU"* (`KAGGLE_BUDGET.md:57`).
In other words RL is a *small* line item precisely because its expensive part (OPE, policy valuation) is
**CPU, offline** — the WIS/ESS/BVFT/SCOPE-RL evaluation in 10.3–10.4 is numpy/CPU work, not GPU work.

The training itself runs on **ONE GPU** by deliberate design, documented in `train_offline_rl.py:36-38`:

> *"the Q-net is tiny (state_dim × 3 actions). Multi-GPU scatter/gather overhead would be LARGER than the
> compute, so RL deliberately runs on ONE GPU with a large batch instead of DataParallel."*

Hence `scale_batch_by_gpus=False` and a large `batch=256`. The teaching point: **model size, not dataset
size, decides the parallelization strategy here** — a two-layer 256-wide MLP with three outputs is so small
that data-parallel communication would dominate, so the correct engineering choice is a single GPU with a
big batch. This also keeps WS5 comfortably inside the ≤30 GPU-h/week constraint (**C3**, `_CANON.md §5`).
These budget figures are **planning-level**, re-confirmed on the live quota panel at build (`_CANON.md §8`).

## 10.7 Results

**Not measured.** No TRINETRA RL policy has been trained; no RL logs have been collected; no OPE verdict,
return, CVaR, or constraint-violation rate exists for TRINETRA. The numpy OPE gate and rule baseline *run*
and are covered by the 128-test suite (`[CONFIRMED]` they execute correctly), but that confirms *the gate
logic*, not *a policy's value*. Every performance figure in this chapter (the D4RL numbers in 10.5, the
PIER/FAITH/GREAT-EER figures in the research artifacts) is **source-reported from the cited paper on that
paper's own benchmark** and must never be read as a TRINETRA result (`_CANON.md §0`,`§1`). The honest
headline is: *the RL component is specified, partially implemented (numpy gate + compile-clean CQL), and
gated — it has not been evaluated.*

## 10.8 Failure modes and mitigations

The research program catalogues the RL-specific failure modes; each has a concrete mitigation already
reflected in the design or code:

- **Reward inversion / reward hacking.** A proxy reward that is cheap to game can drive the policy to a
  degenerate "silence everything" or "alarm always" solution. *Mitigations:* keep reward
  **potential-based and time-invariant** or prove the exception (PBRS, 2608.08158 §2.7, in a partially
  observed MDP); price false alarms above a flat penalty to block cry-wolf (DC-18); audit proxy rewards with
  scarce expert labels via envelope sampling with bounded regret (2610.11281); and govern the reward with an
  **anchor-guarded inspectable verifier** — *a downstream task score CANNOT certify the reward/verifier*
  (2610.11464). The code-level backstop is that the reward is the *logged* `r`, not a learned signal the
  policy can manipulate.
- **Distribution shift (OOD actions).** The core offline-RL failure (2005.01643). *Mitigations:* CQL's
  conservative penalty pushes Q down on OOD actions (10.3.1); IQL's "never query OOD actions" is the
  alternative; one-step improvement avoids iterative error exploitation (2106.08909).
- **OPE positivity violation / ESS collapse → fail-safe.** If the logging policy almost never took some
  action, or weights concentrate, OPE cannot honestly estimate value. *Mitigation — implemented:*
  `ope_feasible` returns `False` (positivity `min_prob=1e-2`, ESS `min_ess_frac=0.1`), so `ope_admission`
  sets `deploy_learned=False` and the system **keeps `RuleBaselinePolicy`** (`rl.py:57-83`). The fail-safe
  is not a slogan — it is the default return path when OPE is untrustworthy.
- **Shield unrealizability / conflicting predicates (FM-05).** Hard physics predicates could contradict each
  other, making no action satisfy the floor. *Mitigation:* realizability-check the shield before deploy
  (2507.23603, `FEATURES.md` F-06); provide a **minimum-predicted-peak-harm fallback** when no safe action
  exists (FAITH 2610.12432).
- **Hollow safety / sim-to-real gap.** A catastrophe-rate drop with no *anticipation* evidence is hollow
  (2609.34041); simulator success need not transfer. *Mitigations:* probe lead-time/anticipation explicitly
  (DC-16); validate against real fire progression (PyroStack) and behavior (FLARE); report **worst-case**
  (not average) constraint violations and rliable-style aggregates with many seeds (`rl_evaluation_plan.md`).
- **Naive RL underperforming a good baseline.** *"RL beats baselines only sometimes; naive RL
  underperforms"* (2509.19972; `FINAL_REPORT.md §7`). *Mitigation:* the whole admission regime — RL must
  **beat a strong non-RL baseline** (MILP bound, GREAT-EER 2602.14676) *and* clear the OPE gate, else the
  honest outcome recorded is "use the non-RL optimizer" (`rl_evaluation_plan.md §1`).

The common thread: **every failure mode degrades to the rule baseline or a bounded-harm fallback**, never to
a silent or unbounded action — the compiled meaning of Rule 19.

---

## 10.9 Open consistency points for the handover

Flagged plainly (per the honesty contract, `00_README §0.5`):

1. **Action-cardinality mismatch.** `offline_rl.py` uses 3 actions `{HOLD,WATCH,ALARM}`; `rl.py`'s
   `RuleBaselinePolicy.act` is binary `{0,1}`. The OPE comparison in `train_offline_rl.py` compares a
   3-action target against a behavior whose default uniform prob is `1/len(ACTIONS)` — the HOLD/WATCH/ALARM
   → binary mapping used when comparing to the rule baseline is **not explicit in code**. `[LIKELY]`
   reconciled by `{WATCH,ALARM}→alarm`, but a reader should verify at build.
2. **CQL vs TD3-BC labeling.** `FEATURES.md` F-06 says "TD3-BC baseline-first"; the implemented Model 6 is
   **CQL** (one-step at `γ=0`). Consistent in spirit; worth a one-line reconciliation in `FEATURES.md`.
3. **Shield object not in numpy core.** The monotone floor lives in `CQLPolicy.act` (torch); `rl.py` has no
   standalone shield class and the realizability check (2507.23603) is specified, **not implemented**.
4. **Baseline = logged behavior reward.** `ope_admission` is called with `baseline_rewards=rewards`
   (the behavior policy's own realized reward). This is a *conservative, self-consistent* comparator
   (`v_b = mean(logged r)`), but it is the *behavior* baseline, not necessarily the *rule baseline's*
   simulated reward — a deliberate but documentable choice.

# 11 — Training Compute: The Kaggle Budget, Multi-GPU Scripts, and Resume Logic

This chapter is the operational contract for *where and how* TRINETRA (HIMKAVACH) deep models get trained.
There is exactly one build platform — **Kaggle GPU notebooks** — and it is small, quota-metered, and
session-limited. Everything here exists to make a research-grade build fit inside roughly **25.5 usable
GPU-hours per week** without ever overstating what that buys.

Read §0.1 before trusting any number in this chapter.

---

## 11.0 Status of every number here (read first)

Two honesty facts govern this entire chapter, and both come straight from `_CANON.md §2` and §8 and from
`KAGGLE_BUDGET.md §0`:

1. **No model has been trained and no dataset has been downloaded.** The PyTorch `deep/` layer and the

## 11.4 Multi-GPU training on T4×2 (as written in code — UNTESTED on a GPU)

> Everything in this section is **UNTESTED**: the scripts are `py_compile`-clean only and were **not
> executed on a GPU** in this environment (`_CANON.md §2`). The behaviour described is what the code *will
> do*, read directly from `trinetra/src/trinetra/deep/train.py`, `ddp.py`, and `kaggle/README.md`.

### 11.4.1 DataParallel is the default path

`train.py` is tuned for Kaggle **T4×2**. By default it uses **both GPUs via `nn.DataParallel`**. On startup
every classifier/anomaly/geo script prints a banner like:

```
[trinetra] GPUs visible=2 | DataParallel=True | effective_batch=128 lr=6.00e-04
```

The mechanics, from `TrainConfig` and `train_one_fold` in `train.py`:

- **GPU-scaled batch.** `--batch N` is the **per-GPU** batch. `effective_batch() = batch_size × n_gpus`
  when `scale_batch_by_gpus` is true (the default). Example: `--batch 64` on 2×T4 → effective batch **128**.
- **Linear LR scaling.** `effective_lr() = lr × n_gpus` when `scale_lr_by_gpus` is true (the default) —
  the warmup-free linear scaling rule (Goyal et al. 2017). With base `lr=3e-4`, 2 GPUs → `6.00e-04`.
- **AMP + cuDNN autotune.** `setup_perf()` sets `cudnn.benchmark = True`, enables TF32 matmul, and sets
  float32 matmul precision "high"; `train_one_fold` wraps the step in `torch.cuda.amp.autocast` with a
  `GradScaler`. fp16 AMP is a large speedup on Turing T4s.
- **The whole loss runs multi-GPU.** `_LossModule` wraps `(model, step_fn)` and returns `loss.reshape(1)`
  so `nn.DataParallel` scatters each batch along dim 0, runs `step_fn` per replica, gathers the per-GPU
  losses, and the caller takes `.mean()`. This lets custom losses (PINN PDE residual, Deep-SVDD,
  cost-sensitive BCE) go multi-GPU **without touching `step_fn`**.
- **Safe `drop_last`.** `make_loader` sets `drop_last` only for shuffled (training) loaders **and only when
  `len(ds) >= 2 * effective_batch`** — so DataParallel can split batches evenly across GPUs, but a tiny
  fold will not drop its only batch and train on nothing.

### 11.4.2 The per-script flags

All training scripts accept (per `kaggle/README.md §3` and each script's `argparse`):

- `--batch N` — **per-GPU** batch; effective batch is `N × n_gpus`.
- `--parallel {auto,dp,none}` — `auto` (default) uses DataParallel when `n_gpus() > 1`; `dp` forces it;
  **`none` forces single-GPU**. `TrainConfig.use_dp()` returns true only for `auto`/`dp` *and* `n_gpus() > 1`.

### 11.4.3 Offline-RL deliberately uses ONE GPU

`train_offline_rl.py` sets `TrainConfig(..., scale_batch_by_gpus=False)` and prints
`offline-RL uses 1 GPU (tiny net)`. The in-code rationale: the Q-net is tiny (state_dim × 3 actions), so
multi-GPU scatter/gather overhead would be **larger than the compute itself**. It uses a **large batch**
(`--batch 256` default) on one GPU instead, driving the training loop directly rather than through
`train_one_fold`'s DataParallel path.

### 11.4.4 Geo-PINN autograd caveat

`train_geo_pinn.py` defaults to `--parallel auto`, so DataParallel is on by default. But the Geo-PINN
physics loss uses `autograd.grad` **inside the forward** (`geo_pinn_step`). Per `kaggle/README.md §2b`:
DataParallel runs this per-replica and *usually* works, **but if you hit a thread/autograd error, rerun
with `--parallel none`** (single GPU) or use the DDP launcher. Note also that slope enters the PINN **only
via `D1 = diffusivity_D1(D0, beta_deg)`** — the `D1 = D0/cos²β` bug-guard from `_CANON.md §4` — so the
multi-GPU path must not reintroduce a second slope term.

### 11.4.5 DistributedDataParallel — the max-throughput path (`ddp.py`)

For long runs, `trinetra.deep.ddp` provides a **DistributedDataParallel** launcher: one process per GPU,
no Python-GIL scatter/gather bottleneck, so it is faster than DataParallel. From `ddp.py`:

- `launch_ddp(worker, args)` spawns one process per GPU via `mp.spawn`; **if `world_size < 2` it just runs
  inline on rank 0** (graceful single-device fallback).
- `ddp_setup` uses the **nccl** backend, `MASTER_ADDR=127.0.0.1`, `MASTER_PORT=29500`, and
  `torch.cuda.set_device(rank)`.
- `wrap_ddp(model, rank)` wraps the model as `DDP(..., device_ids=[rank], find_unused_parameters=False)`.
- `ddp_loader` builds a per-rank `DataLoader` with a `DistributedSampler` (each rank sees a **disjoint
  shard**), `pin_memory=True`, `persistent_workers` when workers > 0, and `drop_last=shuffle`.
- `ddp_worker` is a decorator that does setup/cleanup and an all-reduce **barrier** around your
  `fn(rank, world_size, args)`.
- **Save/eval only on rank 0** via `is_main()`. Gradients are all-reduced automatically.

Critical usage constraint from the module docstring and README: use DDP from a **plain `.py` script**, and
**do not initialize CUDA in the notebook first** (don't touch CUDA before `launch_ddp`).

## 11.5 Checkpoint / resume, outputs, dataloader tuning, mixed precision

### 11.5.1 Checkpoint before the wall

From `KAGGLE_BUDGET.md §5` and the ~12 h session limit:

- **Checkpoint to `/kaggle/working` every ≤30 min AND before the ~11 h wall** (one hour of margin before
  the ~12 h hard kill), and **resume on restart**. A run that does not checkpoint before the wall loses all
  its spent quota.
- **Prefer commit / batch runs over interactive** — an interactive notebook that goes idle gets killed on
  the idle timeout, which **wastes quota** (§11.6).

The per-script save behaviour (from the `kaggle/` scripts): each writes per-fold checkpoints to `--out`
(default `/kaggle/working`) — e.g. `geo_pinn_fold{fold}.pt`, `{model}_fold{fold}.pt`,
`anomaly_fold{fold}.pt`, `offline_rl.pt`, `gmf_head.pt`. These are the resume anchors.

### 11.5.2 Output handling (what leaves the notebook)

Per `kaggle/README.md §4`, copy these to the offline edge/gateway runtime:

- `*.pt` checkpoints (per fold + calibrated temperature).
- `*_report.json` — the **honesty report**; **deploy a model ONLY if `"admitted": true`** (Rule 16, enforced
  by `admit_model` in `train.py`).
- `gmf_head_numpy.json` — the GMF residual head serialized to **numpy** so the OFFLINE gateway (no torch)
  can run it via `ws5_fusion_rl.gmf.gmf_fuse(..., head=closure)`. `train_fusion_head.py` even asserts
  **torch/numpy parity** (`abs(t_val - n_val) < 1e-5`) before exporting.

Keep the weekly **working set ≤ ~20 GB** (the persisted-disk assumption, §11.1).

### 11.5.3 DataLoader tuning

From `make_loader` (`train.py`) and `ddp_loader` (`ddp.py`):

- **`pin_memory`** — on (`cfg.pin_memory and torch.cuda.is_available()`); faster host→device copies.
- **`persistent_workers`** — on whenever `num_workers > 0`; avoids re-spawning workers each epoch.
- **`num_workers`** — default **4** (`TrainConfig.num_workers`).
- **`drop_last`** — only for shuffled training loaders and only with ≥2 full effective batches (§11.4.1).

### 11.5.4 Mixed precision

AMP (fp16/bf16) is on by default (`TrainConfig.amp = True`), applied via `autocast` + `GradScaler` with
gradient unscaling before `clip_grad_norm_` (`grad_clip = 1.0`). `KAGGLE_BUDGET.md §5` additionally calls
for **gradient accumulation**, **tiling EO to fit 13–16 GB RAM**, and **caching preprocessed tensors as
Kaggle Datasets** (built in CPU sessions).

## 11.6 Common Kaggle failures and the fixes

| Symptom | Cause | Fix (from `KAGGLE_BUDGET.md §1/§5` + code) |
|---------|-------|--------------------------------------------|
| **CUDA out-of-memory (OOM)** | EO tiles / batch too big for 13–16 GB RAM or 16 GB VRAM | **Tile** the EO input, **stream** rather than stage, use a **smaller `--batch`** (per-GPU), lean on AMP + gradient accumulation. |
| **Idle timeout kills the run** | Interactive notebook went idle | Use **commit / batch runs**, not interactive — idle timeout **wastes quota**. |
| **Quota exhaustion mid-build** | Weekly ~30 GPU-h cap hit | The ≥15% reserve (§11.2) exists for this; if still tight, apply the **cut-list** (§11.7). All non-training work belongs on CPU sessions. |

For the Geo-PINN thread/autograd error under DataParallel, see §11.4.4 (`--parallel none` or DDP).

## 11.7 The prioritized CUT-LIST

If the live quota turns out tighter than the §11.1 assumption, drop work in **this order**
(`KAGGLE_BUDGET.md §6`):

1. **WS2 media fine-tune** — stay zero-shot / rule-based.
2. **Full SSL pretrain** — instead adapt a public checkpoint (SSL4EO-S12 / TerraMind / Prithvi) with PEFT.
3. **GLOF deep models** — fall back to ITS_LIVE-velocity + HMAGLOFDB threshold rules.
4. **Nowcasting ensemble** — collapse to a single few-step model.
5. **FM-comparison breadth** — keep **ONE** foundation model.

**NEVER cut** (these are the credibility of every number — cheap and load-bearing; DC-01/02/03):
- GBDT + persistence baselines,
- spatial-CV,
- cost-loss evaluation,
- conformal calibration.

The cut order is deliberate: it sheds the lowest-trust, highest-cost work first (media fine-tune, full
pretrain) and protects the cheap pieces that make every reported number defensible.

## 11.8 Seed / rigor policy

Reconciling RB-13's **≥100 seeds** mandate with a 25.5 GPU-h/week cap (`KAGGLE_BUDGET.md §4`):

- **≥100 seeds** → applied to the **cheap models that carry the statistical claims**: GBDT, persistence,
  small U-Net, conformal/anomaly heads (seconds-to-minutes each, CPU or trivial GPU).
- **3–5 seeds** → **expensive FM / SSL runs**; report **dispersion + CI** and state plainly that the FM
  comparison is **seed-limited** (no overclaim, Rule 16).
- The **headline skill claim** — beating two baselines under spatial-CV with a calibrated cost-loss — rests
  on the **many-seed cheap models**, so the ≥100-seed mandate is **met where it is load-bearing**.

This is why the admission gate (`admit_model` in `train.py`) beats **climatology** and a **logistic
baseline** on spatial blocks with a confidence interval before any metric may be advertised: the rigor is
concentrated where it is cheap and decisive.
